t: Pan-Arabism holds that the Arabic-speaking peoples from the Maghreb to the Persian Gulf are one people, a view Jurji Zaydan grounded in their common language rather than religion, race or territory.
Every attempt at a pan-Arab state failed: the United Arab Republic of Egypt and Syria, the first actual merger of two independent Arab countries, lasted only from 1958 to 1961.
Its decline is put down to pan-Islamism, sectarian and social divisions, rivalry among Arab leaders and, to a lesser extent, defeat by Israel, above all in the Six-Day War of 1967.
dyk: Egypt kept the name “the United Arab Republic” after Syria left the union in 1961, implying that it remained open to union with other Arab countries, and renamed itself the Arab Republic of Egypt only in 1973.
ev: The Hussein–McMahon Correspondence begins: Britain will support Arab independence if the Mashreq Arabs revolt against the Ottomans
The Sykes–Picot Agreement divides parts of the Mashreq between Britain and France instead of forming an independent Arab state
The League of Arab States is founded
Egypt and Syria merge as the United Arab Republic under Nasser
Syrian army officers carry out a coup and take Syria out of the United Arab Republic
Israel’s victory in the Six-Day War damages pan-Arabism’s credibility
The Arab Maghreb Union is formed in place of a proposed Algeria–Libya union
The fall of the Assad regime ends Ba’athist rule in Syria, which had espoused pan-Arabism

f.thinkers: Jurji Zaydan (1861–1914), who laid its intellectual foundation; Sharif Hussein ibn Ali of Mecca, who first pressed it as a political project; Constantin Zureiq, Sati’ al-Husri, Zaki al-Arsuzi and Michel Aflaq, Syrian thinkers of the 1930s; Aflaq, for long the Ba’ath Party’s chief ideologist; Gamal Abdel Nasser, who made Arab nationalism Egypt’s state policy
f.texts: Jurji Zaydan’s articles of the early 20th century and his historical novels, which told pre-Islamic and Islamic history as one past shared by all Arabs; the Hussein–McMahon Correspondence (1915–1916)
f.ideas: the Arabs form a single nation; their bond of language outweighs religious, racial and territorial bonds; one state of all Arab countries from the Atlantic Ocean to the Arabian Sea; Modern Standard Arabic as the common written and official language; Arab socialism; opposition to Western political involvement in the Arab world; alliances such as the Arab League against outside forces
f.today: eclipsed by nationalist and Islamist ideologies from the late 1980s; espoused by the Ba’athist governments of Iraq and Syria, the latter until the fall of the Assad regime in 2024; it lost its appeal by the 1990s but kept an intellectual hegemony in the Arab world
